newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Islamists worry the powerful military.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Islamists worry the powerful military.

text.p: Turkey's ruling Islamists are worrying secularists with a series of religion-based proposals, such as a relaxation of the ban on female civil servants wearing Moslem headscarves.

Turkey's first Islamist prime minister, Necmettin Erbakan, had generally shied away from ruffling secularist feathers since his Welfare Party gained power as the senior partner in a coalition with the conservative True Path Party last June.

But in a rush of statements during the current Moslem fasting month of Ramadan, Welfare has pledged to build mosques in Istanbul and Ankara, introduce shorter workdays for fasting civil servants and lift the headscarves ban for public servants.

The Turkish republic was founded as a strictly secular state by Kemal Ataturk in 1923 from the crumbling Islam-based Ottoman Empire. Turkey's secularists, most notably the powerful army, are wary of any move they see as a return to Ottoman values.
This week, President Suleyman Demirel held unscheduled talks with top security and army figures over the recent developments.

Political analyst Yavuz Donat, who is close to the president, told Reuters that Demirel would tell the government to watch its step and inform it of the army's concerns, forcing Welfare into a U-turn.
Demirel's meeting with the army top brass caused some speculation of a new military coup. The army staged three coups between 1960 and 1980.
Political analysts dismiss this as scare-mongering.
"It is nonsense. It is amazing how we are so ready to freak out at things, how fascinated we are with the idea of a coup," columnist Mehmet Ali Birand told Reuters.
Conscious of the military's clout, the government has given the armed forces high pay rises.

Religious issues have caused clear strains within the coalition. The media has reported rifts between the coalition partners over the distribution of proceeds from the sale of sheep skins following the Eid al-Fitr sacrifice festival next week and Welfare's wish to send people by a cheaper road route to the Moslem Haj pilgrimage at Mecca in Saudi Arabia.

"I am afraid to say that the Welfare Party wants to bring these issues onto the agenda with political calculations that are far removed from religious belief and feeling. It is abusing the situation," Defence Minister Turhan Tayan, from the True Path wing of the government, told Milliyet daily.
"There is a mistrust of Welfare regarding the basic properties of the republic. I am afraid to say I share this mistrust," Tayan said in a statement to the newspaper.
Welfare members have publicly insisted on going ahead with the plans, but Erbakan has sought to play down the issue.

"The efforts of those trying to hurt the love between Welfare and our heroic army, and the harmony with our coalition partners, are in vain," the state-run Anatolian news agency quoted Erbakan as saying at the weekend.
Welfare has apparently abandoned many of its centrist and anti-Western views since joining government, even its opposition to Turkey's aspirations for European Union membership.
Erbakan, a wily politician, waited 30 years for the top job in politics and grabbed his chance when the two big conservative parties failed to unite after general polls at the end of 1995.
His position is strengthened because True Path is beholden to Welfare over its support in clearing its leader, Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller, of a series of corruption charges.
A recent furore over Islamic sect members tricking girls into sleeping with them to "rid them of sins and evil spirits" has upset Welfare, but not visibly diminished its support.
